quotedTweet.text:
Montaigne at his best

Essays - Book 1, Ch. 50 - "On Democritus and Heraclitus"

a common thread you see across 1000's of years of sages and philosophers...is a flat-out contempt for human nature.

"vain and ridiculous" writes Montaigne...always vanity, pride, and ego -- see Pascal, La Rochefoucauld, King Solomon

best quote I think is this one...Montaigne takes us down another peg. we are too wretched and pathetic to be capable of evil.

Montaigne: "There is not so much misery in us as emptiness, not so much malice as folly. We are not so full of evil as of inanity, nor so wretched as we are base." 

goes back to Diogenes and even to Homer's Odyssey, describing man as wretched some 2500-3000 years ago: 

"For all the creatures that breathe and creep on this earth, none are so wretched as man."
